title: Foraging sea beet on UK coastlines
subtitle: Year-round coastal green; pick young leaves spring to summer
excerpt: Sea beet grows on shingle beaches, sea walls, and coastal waste ground around most of the UK coast. The glossy, thick leaves taste like spinach with a saltier edge. Pick young leaves from spring through summer before the plant runs to seed.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); BSBI species accounts for Beta vulgaris subsp. maritima; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: Sea beet (Beta vulgaris subsp. maritima) grows on shingle beaches, sea walls, cliff bases, and coastal waste ground around most of the UK coastline. The wild ancestor of cultivated beet, chard, and spinach beet, it produces thick, glossy, dark-green leaves with a spinach flavour and a pronounced salty edge. Young leaves from spring through summer are the best pick; older leaves become tougher and more bitter. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
: confirm (1) the thick, glossy, dark-green leaf with a prominent midrib, (2) the coastal shingle or sea-wall
foraging zone
, and (3) the reddish leaf stalk and lower stem. All three must match.
ID features
Leaves: large, thick, glossy, dark green on the upper surface. Prominent whitish midrib. Lower leaves form a rosette at the base; stem leaves are smaller and alternate.
Stem: often reddish or purplish at the base. Grows 30 to 100 cm tall when in full growth.
Habitat: coastal shingle, sea walls, cliff bases, waste ground near the sea. Very rarely found inland.
Flowers (July to September): tiny, green, in long spikes at the top of the plant. Unremarkable; the plant is harvested well before flowering.
Poisonous look-alikes
Sea beet has few toxic UK
look-alike plants

in its coastal habitat. The thick, glossy leaf and reddish stem are fairly distinctive. Escaped cultivated beet growing at the coastal margin is edible and similar; orache (Atriplex) species grow in the same habitat with mealy, grey-green leaves and are also edible. If the leaf is noticeably thicker and glossier than spinach, and the habitat is coastal shingle or sea wall, it is most likely sea beet.
When and how to harvest

Pick from March through July, before the plant produces its flower spikes. Young leaves up to about 15 cm long are the most tender. Snap or snip individual leaves at the stalk; do not remove more than a third of any plant. Sea beet is perennial and regrows from the same base if the growing point is left intact.
After harvesting

Rinse in cold water to remove salt and any grit. Use within 24 hours. The thick leaves hold up well to cooking: steam, stir-fry, or wilt briefly in a pan. The flavour is similar to spinach with a mineral, salty edge that works well with eggs, fish, and cheese. Young leaves can go into salads raw in small amounts.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage from the coastline for personal use. Some coastal habitats are within National Nature Reserves or Marine Protected Areas with their own access rules; check the designation of the site before foraging. Leave at least two-thirds of any plant you harvest from.

rows.symptom: Leaves are very tough even when young
rows.cause: The plant is mature and has already set flower spikes, or the leaves taken are from the main stem rather than the basal rosette
rows.fix: Select leaves from the lower rosette rather than from the upper stem. If the plant is already in flower, move to a younger plant.

rows.symptom: Leaves taste very bitter after cooking
rows.cause: Older leaves, or the plant has been stressed by drought or salt spray
rows.fix: Blanch in fresh water for two to three minutes, drain, and rinse before using. Older leaves benefit from this treatment; young leaves need it less.
